title: Space Agencies Are Trying to Keep Astronauts From Losing Their Sight
gist: The European Space Agency has commissioned UK startup Siloton to shrink optical-coherence retinal scanning onto a coin-sized photonic chip, because spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) already affects ~70% of ISS astronauts and current ISS eye-scanning hardware is bulky and needs real-time ground guidance that deep-space comms delays will make impossible. Siloton's cofounder frames the space contract as dual-use R&D that directly upgrades its NHS at-home self-scanning product for elderly retinal patients.

insights.claim: Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) affects roughly 70 percent of astronauts aboard the International Space Station according to NASA, making eye degradation a near-universal rather than edge-case crew health problem.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A ~70% incidence rate turns astronaut vision into a budgeted, recurring procurement line for every crewed program, not a research curiosity — a durable demand signal for space-medicine hardware suppliers.

insights.claim: NASA astronaut John Phillips launched to the ISS in 2005 with 20/20 vision and returned six months later at 20/100 — moderate visual impairment — after fluid pooled in his head, squashed his eyeballs, swelled the optic nerve and pushed the retina forward.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A documented 20/20-to-20/100 loss over just six months sets the severity benchmark planners must price for on multi-year Mars-class missions.
insights.quote: launched to the ISS in 2005 with 20/20 vision, and splashed down six months later with his vision at 20/100
insights.locator: One of the starkest cases is that of NASA astronaut

insights.claim: The mechanism of SANS is mechanical rather than radiological — in microgravity bodily fluid, uninhibited by gravity, accumulates in the head and physically deforms the eyeball and optic nerve — which means shielding and radiation countermeasures do not address it.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Separates the SANS problem from the radiation-mitigation market: the addressable solutions are diagnostics, fluid-shift countermeasures and artificial gravity, not shielding materials.
insights.quote: bodily fluid, uninhibited by gravity, built up in his head, squashing his eyeballs, swelling his optic nerve, and pushing his retina forward
insights.locator: While he was in space, bodily fluid

insights.claim: Space agencies weigh two distinct SANS costs — the operational risk of an astronaut losing vision mid-mission and the long-term health liability after return — and returning to Earth only reverses some of the damage.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Partial irreversibility means agencies cannot defer the problem to post-flight care, which forces in-flight diagnostic spend now rather than after Artemis flies.
insights.quote: While returning to Earth can reverse some of the damage, space agencies are concerned by both the operational risk of astronauts losing their vision mid-mission, as well as the longer-term health impacts.

insights.claim: The existing ISS eye-monitoring device — a modified optometry instrument measuring the thickness of layers at the back of the eye — is bulky and requires real-time remote guidance from experts on the ground, a dependency that breaks as deep-space communication delays lengthen.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Light-speed latency is the forcing function creating a new product category: every ground-in-the-loop medical instrument on ISS becomes an obsolete SKU once missions leave cislunar space.
insights.quote: the device is bulky and requires real-time remote guidance from experts on the ground

insights.claim: Siloton's pitch is automation of the scan workflow so examinations need no ground support, letting astronauts self-scan retinas far more frequently and generating a denser longitudinal dataset the ESA hopes will surface early warning signs before any vision change occurs.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: The value accrues to the data cadence, not the optics — whoever owns the longitudinal ocular dataset owns the eventual predictive/treatment IP for SANS.
insights.quote: possibly provide early warning signs that changes in the eye may be occurring—even before they result in vision change

insights.claim: Spaceflight-grade eye scanning faces hard engineering constraints beyond optics: batteries are largely disallowed because of fire risk, the binocular-sized unit competes for scarce cabin volume, and head stabilization normally provided by a gravity-dependent chin rest must be re-engineered.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Power, volume and restraint constraints — not imaging performance — are the real moat and the real schedule risk for any terrestrial medtech trying to sell into crewed spaceflight.
insights.quote: Other technical challenges include getting around using batteries to power the device because they pose such a big fire risk.

insights.claim: Siloton, founded by physicists in 2020, uses quantum technology to shrink the core components of optometrist-grade eye-testing equipment onto a photonic chip smaller than a coin — a size and cost step-change versus benchtop retinal imaging hardware.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Chip-scale retinal imaging is the enabling shift that opens home and remote-care diagnostics markets far larger than the space niche; watch photonic-integration plays for the same collapse in instrument BOM cost.
insights.quote: uses quantum technology to shrink core components used in eye-testing equipment found at optometrists to fit on a photonic chip smaller than a coin
insights.locator: The health tech uses quantum technology

insights.claim: Siloton is already building the same capability for the UK's National Health Service so retinal-condition patients can self-scan at home, and its CTO Euan Allen says the ESA's requirements are essentially identical, just in a different environment.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: One R&D stack serving two funded buyers — a national health system and a space agency — means the space contract is effectively non-dilutive development capital for a much bigger terrestrial TAM.
insights.quote: The ESA pretty much has the same requirements

insights.claim: Allen argues the hard usability problem is terrestrial, not orbital: getting an 80-year-old patient with existing visual impairment to self-scan is harder than getting a young, highly trained astronaut with full eye function to do it.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Inverts the usual assumption that space qualification is the gating risk — if the NHS elderly-patient use case is the harder validation, execution risk sits in the commercial channel, not the ESA contract.
insights.quote: We're very confident, because we're trying to do that with 80-year-old patients who already have some level of visual imparity
insights.locator: But that’s a walk-in-the-park compared with getting a retiree

insights.claim: Allen expects bidirectional technology bleed-through, with space-hardening work improving the NHS home device and vice versa, framing the ESA program as a product-quality subsidy rather than a standalone revenue line.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Classic dual-use flywheel: judge such companies on whether agency contracts measurably harden the commercial product, not on contract value alone.
insights.quote: All this research and development work, in principle, is making our products that are going to go into the NHS much better.
insights.locator: I think lots of the stuff that we're doing for space

insights.claim: The ESA commissioned Siloton's solution specifically ahead of the international Artemis moon flights and other deep-space missions, and the UK Space Agency's director Rebecca Evernden publicly calls SANS a serious health risk for long missions.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Artemis timelines put a dated procurement window on crew-health hardware, and UK agency endorsement signals national-level funding support behind small British space-medtech suppliers.
insights.quote: The eye condition SANS is a serious health risk facing astronauts on long missions
